sentences.text: Users hate passwords.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: They forget them, reuse them, write them on sticky notes, and complain when forced to create new ones.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Organizations hate passwords too—they generate helpdesk tickets, create security vulnerabilities, and frustrate users.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Single Sign-On (SSO) emerged as the solution: authenticate once, access everything.↵The promise sounds simple, but the reality is complex.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Over decades, multiple SSO technologies emerged, each solving different problems in different contexts.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Windows Integrated Authentication (WIA) worked within corporate networks.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Kerberos provided secure authentication for distributed systems.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SPNEGO bridged Windows and web applications.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML enabled enterprise federation.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth revolutionized API authorization.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OpenID Connect (OIDC) finally unified authentication and authorization for modern applications.↵This exploration traces SSO's evolution from 1980s network authentication to today's cloud-native protocols.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Understanding this history reveals why we have so many SSO standards, when to use each one, and how to avoid common authentication mistakes that compromise security.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Before examining SSO solutions, understanding the problem they solve is essential.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Passwords create friction and risk in every system.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Passwords seemed like a good idea initially:↵:::error{title="Password Problems"}↵**User Burden**↵Remember dozens of passwords↵Different complexity requirements↵Frequent expiration policies↵Password reset friction↵**Security Risks**↵Password reuse across systems↵Weak passwords to aid memory↵Phishing attacks steal credentials↵Credential stuffing attacks↵**Operational Costs**↵Helpdesk password reset tickets↵Account lockout issues↵Provisioning complexity↵Audit trail gaps↵A typical enterprise employee manages passwords for email, file shares, databases, web applications, VPN, and countless SaaS tools.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Each system has different requirements—minimum length, special characters, expiration periods.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Users respond predictably: they reuse passwords, write them down, or use simple patterns like "Password1", "Password2", "Password3".↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Single Sign-On addresses these problems:↵:::success{title="SSO Benefits"}↵**User Experience**↵Authenticate once per session↵Access all authorized systems↵Reduced password fatigue↵Faster application access↵**Security Improvements**↵Centralized authentication↵Stronger authentication methods↵Consistent security policies↵Better audit trails↵**Operational Efficiency**↵Fewer helpdesk tickets↵Simplified provisioning↵Centralized access control↵Reduced administrative overhead↵The vision is compelling: users authenticate once in the morning, then seamlessly access email, file shares, databases, and web applications without additional logins.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Security improves because authentication happens in one place with strong controls.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Operations simplify because access management centralizes.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The first practical SSO implementations emerged in the 1980s and 1990s, designed for corporate networks.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Kerberos, developed at MIT in the 1980s, provided secure authentication for distributed systems:↵:::anote{title="🎫 Kerberos Fundamentals"}↵**Core Concept**↵Ticket-based authentication↵Trusted third party (KDC)↵No passwords sent over network↵Mutual authentication↵**How It Works**↵User authenticates to KDC↵KDC issues Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)↵User requests service ticket using TGT↵User presents service ticket to application↵Application validates ticket with KDC↵Kerberos solved a critical problem: how to authenticate users across a network without sending passwords.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The protocol uses symmetric key cryptography and a trusted Key Distribution Center (KDC).

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The name "Kerberos" comes from Greek mythology—the three-headed dog guarding the underworld, representing the client, server, and KDC working together.↵:::↵ ↵:::tip{title="Deep Dive: Kerberos"}↵For detailed coverage of Kerberos architecture, authentication flows, ticket structure, security considerations, and implementation guidance, see Understanding Kerberos: Network Authentication Explained.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Microsoft built on Kerberos for Windows domain authentication:↵:::anote{title="🪟 Windows Authentication Evolution"}↵**NTLM (NT LAN Manager)**↵Challenge-response protocol↵No trusted third party↵Vulnerable to relay attacks↵Legacy protocol, still supported↵**Kerberos in Active Directory**↵Default since Windows 2000↵Active Directory as KDC↵Seamless desktop SSO↵Works with Windows applications↵Windows Integrated Authentication (WIA) provides transparent SSO within corporate networks.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: When you log into your Windows workstation with domain credentials, you authenticate to Active Directory using Kerberos.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Your workstation caches tickets.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: When you access a file share, intranet website, or other Windows-integrated application, your workstation automatically presents the appropriate ticket.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: You never see another login prompt—it just works.↵This seamless experience set user expectations for SSO.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Employees wondered why they needed separate logins for web applications when their desktop applications worked without additional authentication.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SPNEGO (Simple and Protected GSSAPI Negotiation Mechanism) extended Windows authentication to web browsers:↵:::anote{title="SPNEGO for Web SSO"}↵**Purpose**↵Extend Kerberos to HTTP↵Browser negotiates authentication↵Transparent to users↵Intranet SSO↵**How It Works**↵Browser requests protected resource↵Server responds with WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate↵Browser requests Kerberos ticket↵Browser sends ticket in Authorization header↵Server validates ticket and grants access↵**Requirements**↵Domain-joined workstation↵Kerberos-enabled browser↵Server in trusted zone↵Proper DNS/SPN configuration↵SPNEGO enabled intranet web applications to use Windows authentication.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: An employee accessing the company portal wouldn't see a login page—the browser automatically authenticated using their Windows credentials.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This worked beautifully within corporate networks but failed outside them.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Remote employees, mobile devices, and external partners couldn't use Windows authentication, creating a gap that later protocols would fill.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: As organizations adopted web applications and cloud services, they needed SSO beyond corporate networks.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML emerged as the enterprise federation standard.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) enables SSO across organizational boundaries:↵:::anote{title="SAML Core Concepts"}↵**Entities**↵Identity Provider (IdP): Authenticates users↵Service Provider (SP): Provides applications↵User: Accesses applications↵**Key Features**↵Digitally signed XML assertions↵Browser-based redirect flows↵Works across organizational boundaries↵Mature enterprise standard↵SAML separates authentication from application access.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The Identity Provider (IdP) handles authentication—verifying who you are.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Service Providers (SPs) trust the IdP's assertions about your identity.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: When you access a SAML-enabled application, it redirects you to your organization's IdP.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: You authenticate once at the IdP, which issues a SAML assertion—a digitally signed XML document stating who you are and what attributes you have.↵:::↵

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML became the standard for enterprise SSO:↵:::success{title="SAML Strengths"}↵**Enterprise Adoption**↵Supported by major SaaS vendors↵Works across organizational boundaries↵Mature, well-understood protocol↵Strong security properties↵**Use Cases**↵Employee access to SaaS applications↵Partner federation↵Customer federation (B2B)↵Academic federation (Shibboleth)↵Organizations deploy SAML to provide employees seamless access to dozens of SaaS applications.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: An employee authenticates to their corporate IdP (often Active Directory Federation Services or Okta), then accesses Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, and other applications without additional logins.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Despite widespread adoption, SAML has limitations:↵:::error{title="SAML Challenges"}↵**Technical Complexity**↵XML-based, verbose↵Complex configuration↵Certificate management overhead↵Difficult to debug↵**Mobile and API Limitations**↵Designed for browser-based flows↵Poor mobile app support↵Not designed for API authorization↵Requires browser redirects↵SAML works well for browser-based enterprise applications but struggles with modern use cases.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Mobile apps can't easily handle browser redirects.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: APIs need authorization without user interaction.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Single-page applications want JSON, not XML.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: These limitations created space for new protocols.↵:::↵:::tip{title="Deep Dive: SAML"}↵For detailed coverage of SAML architecture, authentication flows, security best practices, and implementation guidance, see Understanding SAML: Enterprise Federation Explained.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: As web applications evolved into API-driven architectures, a new problem emerged: how to grant third-party applications limited access to user resources without sharing passwords.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Before OAuth, applications used password sharing:↵:::error{title="Password Anti-Pattern"}↵**The Problem**↵User gives password to third-party app↵App has full access to account↵No way to revoke access without changing password↵Password exposed to multiple parties↵**Example**↵Photo printing service needs access to photos↵User provides email password↵Service downloads all emails↵Service stores password↵User can't revoke access selectively↵This pattern was common but dangerous.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Users shared passwords with multiple services, each gaining full account access.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: If one service was compromised, all services were at risk.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Users couldn't revoke access to one service without changing their password and updating all services.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth 2.0 solved the delegation problem:↵:::anote{title="OAuth Core Concepts"}↵**Entities**↵Resource Owner: User who owns data↵Client: Application requesting access↵Authorization Server: Issues tokens↵Resource Server: Hosts protected resources↵**Tokens**↵Access Token: Grants API access↵Refresh Token: Obtains new access tokens↵Scope: Limits permissions↵Expiration: Time-limited access↵**Key Principle**↵Never share passwords↵Grant limited access↵Revocable permissions↵Time-limited tokens↵OAuth enables delegation without password sharing.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: When a photo printing service needs access to your photos, it redirects you to your photo service's authorization server.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: You authenticate and approve specific permissions—"allow read access to photos." The authorization server issues an access token to the printing service.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This token grants limited access (only photos, not emails) for a limited time.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: You can revoke the token anytime without changing your password.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth defines multiple flows for different scenarios:↵:::anote{title="OAuth Grant Types"}↵**Authorization Code Flow**↵For web applications with backend↵Most secure flow↵Uses client secret↵Recommended for confidential clients↵**Implicit Flow**↵For browser-based apps (deprecated)↵No client secret↵Token in URL fragment↵Security concerns led to deprecation↵**Client Credentials Flow**↵For machine-to-machine↵No user interaction↵Service account authentication↵Backend services↵**Resource Owner Password Flow**↵User provides credentials to client↵Legacy migration path↵Not recommended↵Defeats OAuth purpose↵The Authorization Code Flow is the gold standard.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The client redirects the user to the authorization server, receives an authorization code, then exchanges that code for an access token using its client secret.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This flow keeps tokens away from the browser and provides strong security.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth became ubiquitous:↵:::success{title="OAuth Adoption"}↵**Consumer Applications**↵"Sign in with Google"↵"Connect to Facebook"↵"Authorize Twitter access"↵Third-party integrations↵**API Authorization**↵Microservices authentication↵Mobile app backend access↵Partner API access↵IoT device authorization↵OAuth powers the "Sign in with Google" buttons across the web.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: It enables Spotify to post to Facebook, fitness apps to sync with health platforms, and countless integrations between services.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth's success came from solving a real problem—secure delegation—with a practical solution.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth solved authorization but created confusion about authentication:↵:::error{title="OAuth Authentication Confusion"}↵**OAuth is NOT Authentication**↵OAuth grants access to resources↵Doesn't verify user identity↵Access token doesn't identify user↵Using OAuth for authentication is risky↵**The Problem**↵Developers misused OAuth for login↵Security vulnerabilities emerged↵No standard user info endpoint↵Inconsistent implementations↵Developers saw OAuth's success and tried using it for authentication.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: They'd get an access token and assume it identified the user.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This created security problems—access tokens aren't designed to prove identity.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Different providers implemented user info endpoints differently.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The ecosystem needed a standard authentication layer on top of OAuth.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OpenID Connect (OIDC) built on OAuth 2.0 to provide standardized authentication.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OpenID Connect solved the authentication problem OAuth wasn't designed for:↵:::anote{title="🆔 OIDC Core Innovation"}↵**The Problem**↵Developers misused OAuth for authentication↵Access tokens aren't identity proof↵Inconsistent user info implementations↵Security vulnerabilities↵**OIDC Solution**↵Adds ID Token (JWT) to OAuth↵ID Token proves user identity↵Standardizes user information↵Combines authentication + authorization↵**Key Benefits**↵JSON instead of XML↵Mobile and API friendly↵Simple developer experience↵Modern architecture support↵OIDC extends OAuth by adding an ID Token—a JWT containing identity claims.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: When you authenticate with OIDC, you receive both an ID Token (proving who you are) and an access token (granting API access).

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This clear separation eliminates confusion and provides secure authentication.↵:::↵

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OIDC became the modern SSO standard:↵:::success{title="OIDC Adoption"}↵**Use Cases**↵Web application login↵Mobile app authentication↵API authorization↵Microservices security↵**Providers**↵Auth0, Okta, Azure AD↵Google Identity Platform↵AWS Cognito↵Self-hosted: Keycloak, ORY Hydra↵OIDC powers modern authentication across web apps, mobile apps, and APIs.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Developers integrate using standard libraries, avoiding custom authentication code.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: :::tip{title="OIDC vs SAML Decision"}↵**Choose SAML When:**↵Legacy enterprise app integration↵Vendor only supports SAML↵Existing SAML infrastructure↵**Choose OIDC When:**↵Building new applications↵Mobile app authentication↵API authorization needed↵Modern architecture↵**Reality:**↵Many IdPs support both↵Use OIDC for new projects↵Keep SAML for legacy integrations↵SAML isn't going away, but new projects should use OIDC.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: It's simpler, more flexible, and better suited to modern architectures.↵:::↵:::tip{title="Deep Dive: OpenID Connect"}↵For detailed coverage of OIDC architecture, authentication flows, ID tokens, security best practices, and implementation guidance, see OpenID Connect: Modern Authentication Explained.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: With multiple SSO technologies available, how do you choose?

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Use this framework to guide your choice:↵:::tip{title="SSO Technology Selection"}↵**Kerberos/WIA When:**↵Windows-only environment↵Corporate network access↵Desktop applications↵Intranet websites↵No external access needed↵**SPNEGO When:**↵Extending Kerberos to web↵Intranet applications↵Windows-integrated auth↵Domain-joined devices↵**SAML When:**↵Enterprise SaaS integration↵Vendor requires SAML↵B2B federation↵Legacy application support↵Browser-based flows only↵**OAuth When:**↵API authorization↵Third-party integrations↵Delegated access↵No authentication needed↵**OIDC When:**↵Modern web applications↵Mobile applications↵API authorization + authentication↵Microservices↵New development↵The decision depends on your context.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: A corporate intranet might use Kerberos.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: An enterprise SaaS integration uses SAML.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: A modern web application uses OIDC.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: An API integration uses OAuth.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Teams make predictable mistakes with SSO:↵:::error{title="SSO Anti-Patterns"}↵**Using OAuth for Authentication**↵OAuth is for authorization↵Not designed to prove identity↵Security vulnerabilities↵Use OIDC instead↵**Implementing Custom SSO**↵"We'll build our own"↵Security vulnerabilities↵Maintenance burden↵Use standard protocols↵**Ignoring Token Security**↵Storing tokens in localStorage↵Long-lived tokens↵No token rotation↵Inadequate validation↵**Poor Session Management**↵No logout functionality↵Session fixation vulnerabilities↵Inconsistent session lifetimes↵No single logout↵The most common mistake is using OAuth for authentication instead of OIDC.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Developers see OAuth's popularity and try to authenticate users with access tokens.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This creates security problems.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Use OIDC for authentication—it's designed for that purpose.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Seeing how organizations actually implement SSO clarifies the differences:

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: A large corporation's intranet uses Kerberos:↵:::anote{title="🏢 Corporate Intranet"}↵**Context**↵10,000 employees↵Windows domain environment↵Intranet applications↵File shares and databases↵Desktop applications↵**Implementation**↵Active Directory as KDC↵Windows Integrated Authentication↵SPNEGO for web applications↵Seamless desktop SSO↵No additional logins↵**Why It Works**↵Homogeneous Windows environment↵Corporate network access↵Desktop-focused workflows↵Existing AD infrastructure↵Transparent to users↵Employees log into their workstations once.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: They access file shares, intranet sites, and desktop applications without additional authentication.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Kerberos handles everything transparently.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This works because the environment is controlled—Windows devices, corporate network, trusted applications.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: An enterprise integrating SaaS applications uses SAML:↵:::anote{title="☁️ SaaS Integration"}↵**Context**↵5,000 employees↵50+ SaaS applications↵Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, etc.↵Need centralized access control↵Compliance requirements↵**Implementation**↵Okta as SAML IdP↵SAML federation with each SaaS app↵Employee portal for app access↵Centralized provisioning↵Audit logging↵**Why It Works**↵SaaS vendors support SAML↵Browser-based applications↵Centralized authentication↵Simplified access management↵Compliance requirements met↵Employees authenticate to Okta once, then access all SaaS applications without additional logins.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: IT manages access centrally—provision new employees, deprovision departing employees, enforce security policies.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML enables this federation across organizational boundaries.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: A startup building a web application uses OIDC:↵:::anote{title="Modern Web Application"}↵**Context**↵SaaS product for businesses↵Web and mobile applications↵RESTful API backend↵Microservices architecture↵Need authentication and API authorization↵**Implementation**↵Auth0 as OIDC provider↵Authorization Code Flow with PKCE↵JWT access tokens for API↵Refresh token rotation↵Standard OIDC libraries↵**Why It Works**↵Modern architecture↵Mobile and web support↵API authorization built-in↵Developer-friendly↵Security best practices↵Users authenticate with OIDC, receiving an ID Token and access token.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The web app validates the ID Token for authentication.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The mobile app uses the access token for API calls.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Microservices validate JWT tokens.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OIDC provides authentication and authorization in one protocol, fitting modern architectures perfectly.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SSO improves security but introduces new risks:

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Tokens require careful handling:↵:::warning{title="Token Security Best Practices"}↵**Storage**↵Never store tokens in localStorage↵Use httpOnly cookies when possible↵Encrypt tokens at rest↵Clear tokens on logout↵**Transmission**↵Always use HTTPS↵Validate TLS certificates↵Avoid tokens in URLs↵Use secure headers↵**Validation**↵Verify token signatures↵Check expiration↵Validate issuer↵Verify audience↵**Rotation**↵Short-lived access tokens↵Refresh token rotation↵Revocation mechanisms↵Monitor for abuse↵Tokens are bearer credentials—anyone with the token can use it.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Storing tokens in localStorage exposes them to XSS attacks.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Long-lived tokens increase risk if compromised.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Always validate tokens properly—check signatures, expiration, issuer, and audience.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SSO creates a single point of failure:↵:::warning{title="SSO Availability Risks"}↵**The Problem**↵IdP outage blocks all access↵No fallback authentication↵Business continuity risk↵Dependency on external service↵**Mitigation**↵High availability IdP deployment↵Disaster recovery planning↵Emergency access procedures↵SLA monitoring↵Consider multi-IdP setup↵When your IdP goes down, users can't access anything.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: This makes IdP availability critical.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Deploy IdPs with high availability, plan for disasters, and establish emergency access procedures.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Some organizations deploy multiple IdPs for redundancy.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SSO complicates session management:↵:::warning{title="Session Management Challenges"}↵**Multiple Sessions**↵IdP session↵Application sessions↵Different lifetimes↵Logout complexity↵**Single Logout**↵Logging out of one app↵Should log out of all apps↵Requires coordination↵Often incomplete↵**Best Practices**↵Implement single logout↵Consistent session lifetimes↵Clear session on browser close↵Monitor active sessions↵Users expect that logging out of one application logs them out of everything.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Implementing this requires coordination between the IdP and all applications.

sentences.text: Single Sign-On evolved from corporate network authentication to cloud-native protocols over three decades.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Kerberos provided secure network authentication in the 1980s.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Windows Integrated Authentication extended this to desktop environments.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SPNEGO bridged Windows authentication to web browsers.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML enabled enterprise federation across organizational boundaries.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth solved API authorization and delegation.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OpenID Connect unified authentication and authorization for modern applications.↵Each technology emerged to solve specific problems in specific contexts.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Kerberos works for corporate networks with Windows infrastructure.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SAML works for enterprise SaaS integration with browser-based flows.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OAuth works for API authorization and third-party integrations.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: OIDC works for modern web and mobile applications needing both authentication and authorization.↵Common mistakes include using OAuth for authentication instead of OIDC, implementing custom SSO instead of using standard protocols, poor token security practices, and inadequate session management.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: These mistakes compromise security and create maintenance burdens.↵The decision between SSO technologies depends on your context.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Corporate intranets use Kerberos.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Modern web applications use OIDC.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: API integrations use OAuth.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Many organizations use multiple protocols—SAML for legacy applications, OIDC for new development.↵Security considerations include token security, single point of failure risks, and session management complexity.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Tokens require careful storage, transmission, validation, and rotation.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: SSO creates availability dependencies that need mitigation.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Session management across multiple applications requires coordination.↵Real-world examples show Kerberos succeeding in corporate intranets, SAML succeeding in enterprise SaaS integration, and OIDC succeeding in modern web applications.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Each technology excels in its appropriate context.↵Before choosing an SSO technology, understand your requirements.

sentences.text: What kind of applications do you have?

sentences.text: The answers to these questions matter more than opinions about which protocol is better.↵The goal isn't perfect adherence to one protocol.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: The goal is secure, usable authentication that enables business objectives.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Use protocols as tools, not goals.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Choose based on your context, implement security best practices, and focus on user experience.↵Whether you choose Kerberos, SAML, OAuth, or OIDC, remember: SSO is a tool for solving authentication problems, not an end in itself.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: Focus on outcomes—secure access, good user experience, operational efficiency.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: If the protocol helps achieve these outcomes, use it.

sourceRef.title: The Evolution of Single Sign-On: From Kerberos to OIDC

sentences.text: If it doesn't, choose differently.
